los.text: Identify what constitutes psychotic illness.
sessions: Case Presentation, Mental State Exam and Classification & Psychopathology of Schizophrenia
los.html:
• Psychosis: loss of contact with reality, with hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder and usually impaired insight.
CategoryExamples
Primary psychotic disordersSchizophrenia (~1% lifetime), schizoaffective disorder, delusional disorder, acute and transient psychotic disorder
Mood disorders with psychosisMania with psychotic features, psychotic depression, postpartum psychosis
Organic (secondary)
  • Delirium
  • Dementia (especially Lewy body)
  • Substances (cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine, alcohol withdrawal, steroids, levodopa)
  • Temporal lobe epilepsy
  • Brain tumour
  • Encephalitis (anti-NMDA)
  • SLE
  • HIV
  • Thyroid disease
  • Cushing's
  • B12 deficiency
Schizophrenia(ICD-11)Persistent delusions, hallucinations, thought disorder, or experiences of influence/passivity/control, plus negative symptoms, for at least 1 month.
Schneider's first-rank symptoms
  • Auditory hallucinations (third-person voices discussing the patient, running commentary, thought echo)
  • Thought alienation (insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting)
  • Passivity (made feelings, impulses, actions; somatic passivity)
  • Delusional perception.
Negative symptomsBlunted affect, alogia (poverty of speech), avolition, anhedonia, social withdrawal; cognitive symptoms (attention, memory, executive function).

los.text: Take a psychiatric history and perform a mental state exam of a psychotic patient and to perform a basic risk assessment.
sessions: Case Presentation, Mental State Exam and Classification & Psychopathology of Schizophrenia
los.html:
HistoryContent
Presenting complaint and HPCOnset and duration, positive symptoms, negative symptoms, prodrome (withdrawal, declining function), mood symptoms, triggers
SubstancesCannabis, stimulants, alcohol
Past psychiatric historyPrevious episodes, admissions, Mental Health Act detentions, medications, adherence, side effects
Medical history and drugsOrganic causes, steroids, levodopa
Family historySchizophrenia, bipolar disorder, suicide
Personal and socialDevelopment, education, relationships, work, housing, finances, support
ForensicViolence, convictions
Premorbid personality, insight
MSE domainPsychosis findings
Appearance and behaviourSelf-neglect, perplexity, guardedness, responding to unseen stimuli, catatonia
SpeechPressured, poverty of speech, neologisms
Mood and affectBlunted/flat or incongruent affect
Thought formLoosening of associations, derailment ("knight's move"), word salad, thought block
Thought contentDelusions (persecutory, reference, grandiose, control, nihilistic), suicidal or homicidal thoughts
PerceptionAuditory hallucinations (second- or third-person, command); visual hallucinations suggest organic causes
CognitionUsually intact in schizophrenia (impaired in delirium)
InsightDo they believe they're unwell? Accept treatment?
  • Basic risk assessment:
RiskFactors
To selfSuicide (~5% lifetime in schizophrenia: highest early in illness, after discharge, with depression, command hallucinations, insight into deterioration), self-harm, self-neglect
To othersCommand hallucinations, persecutory delusions about specific people, substance misuse, previous violence, non-adherence
From othersExploitation, abuse, vulnerability
Protective factorsSupport, engagement, children, hope
  • Formulate and plan: level of risk, crisis plan, observation level, means restriction, involvement of the crisis team, safeguarding.

los.text: Elicit characteristic signs and symptoms in order to assist in the diagnosis of a range of neurotic and psychotic disorders
sessions: Case Presentation, Mental State Exam and Classification & Psychopathology of Schizophrenia
los.html:
DisorderCharacteristic features
Generalised anxiety disorderExcessive worry about many things most days for months, restlessness, muscle tension, poor sleep and concentration, irritability, autonomic symptoms
Panic disorder
  • Recurrent unexpected panic attacks (palpitations, sweating, trembling, breathlessness, chest pain, fear of dying or losing control, peaking within minutes) + worry about further attacks
  • Often with agoraphobia
AgoraphobiaFear and avoidance of situations where escape may be difficult (crowds, public transport, leaving home)
Social anxiety disorderFear of scrutiny, embarrassment or humiliation in social or performance situations
Specific phobiaMarked fear of a specific object or situation (spiders, heights, needles) with avoidance
OCD
  • Obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges: contamination, harm, symmetry) and compulsions (washing, checking, counting, mental rituals) that reduce anxiety
  • Recognised as own thoughts, usually ego-dystonic
PTSDAfter trauma: re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, sense of current threat (hypervigilance, startle)
Adjustment disorderDistress after a stressor, within a month, resolving within months
Bodily distress / health anxietyPersistent distressing bodily symptoms or fear of illness despite reassurance
DepressionLow mood, anhedonia, low energy for ≥2 weeks
Psychotic disordersSee LO 1: hallucinations, delusions, loss of insight
  • Key distinction: in neurotic (anxiety-related) disorders reality testing and insight are preserved (the person knows the fear or thought is excessive)
    • in psychosis they're lost.

los.text: Link pathological processes to the symptoms and signs of neurotic disorders.
sessions: Case Presentation, Mental State Exam and Classification & Psychopathology of Schizophrenia
los.html:
LevelMechanismLink to symptoms
Neural circuitsAmygdala hyperactivity (fear), reduced prefrontal (vmPFC) control, hippocampal changes (context processing; smaller in PTSD)Exaggerated fear responses, difficulty "switching off" fear, intrusive memories
OCD circuitOveractive cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop (orbitofrontal cortex, caudate)Repetitive intrusive thoughts and urges to act
NeurotransmittersSerotonin (SSRIs work), noradrenaline (locus coeruleus: panic, hyperarousal), GABA (benzodiazepines anxiolytic), CRHAutonomic arousal: palpitations, tremor, sweating (sympathetic)
Stress hormonesHPA axis dysregulation (PTSD: enhanced negative feedback, low cortisol)
PhysiologyHyperventilation → respiratory alkalosisParaesthesia, light-headedness, carpopedal spasm, chest tightness in panic
LearningClassical conditioning (fear linked to a cue: phobias, PTSD); avoidance relieves anxiety (negative reinforcement), so the fear never extinguishesAvoidance, safety behaviours
CognitionCatastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations (panic: "I'm having a heart attack"), worry as avoidance (GAD), threat-focused attention, inflated responsibility (OCD)Escalating panic, persistent worry, compulsions
VulnerabilityGenetics (~30–40% heritable), behavioural inhibition temperament, early adversity, life stress (stress–diathesis)

los.text: Link factors in a psychiatric history and mental state examination to identify a diagnosis in a patient with a neurotic disorder.
sessions: Case Presentation, Mental State Exam and Classification & Psychopathology of Schizophrenia
los.html:
• Approach: history (what, when, triggers, avoidance, safety behaviours, impact, duration)
    • MSE
    • screening tools
    • exclude physical causes (hyperthyroidism, caffeine, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, stimulants, hypoglycaemia, arrhythmias, asthma, phaeochromocytoma) and look for comorbid depression and substance misuse.
History and MSE cluesLikely diagnosis
Sudden unprovoked episodes of palpitations, breathlessness and fear of dying; now avoids supermarkets and busesPanic disorder with agoraphobia
Months of constant worry about health, money and family, can't relax, poor sleep, tense muscles; anxious, restlessGAD
Intrusive thoughts of contamination, washes hands for hours, knows it's excessive; chapped red handsOCD
Nightmares and flashbacks since an assault 3 months ago, avoids the area, jumpy and irritablePTSD
Dreads presenting at work, blushes, avoids meetings for fear of embarrassmentSocial anxiety disorder
MSE in neurotic disorders
  • Anxious, restless, sweaty or tremulous
  • Speech normal or rapid
  • Mood anxious
  • Thought content shows worries or obsessions (not delusions)
  • No true hallucinations (flashbacks are re-experiencing)
  • Cognition intact
  • Insight preserved.
ToolsGAD-7, PHQ-9, PCL-5 (PTSD), Y-BOCS (OCD).

los.text: Link neural pathways, and pharmacological reagents which act upon them, to the occurrence and treatment of psychosis
sessions: Management of schizophrenia and rapid tranquillisation
los.html:
Dopamine pathwayRole in psychosisEffect of D₂ blockade
Mesolimbic (VTA → nucleus accumbens/limbic system)Overactivity → positive symptomsTreats hallucinations and delusions
Mesocortical (VTA → prefrontal cortex)Underactivity → negative and cognitive symptomsMay worsen negative symptoms
Nigrostriatal (substantia nigra → striatum)Motor controlExtrapyramidal side effects: acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia
Tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus → pituitary)Dopamine inhibits prolactinHyperprolactinaemia: galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis
  • Other systems: glutamate (NMDA hypofunction) (ketamine and PCP cause psychosis), serotonin 5-HT₂A (LSD causes hallucinations; atypicals block 5-HT₂A → fewer EPSEs)
    • stimulants (amphetamines, cocaine) and cannabis raise psychosis risk.
DrugNotesKey side effects
Typical (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, flupentixol, zuclopenthixol depot)Potent D₂ blockadeEPSEs, prolactin, QT (haloperidol)
OlanzapineAtypicalWeight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, sedation
RisperidoneAtypicalHyperprolactinaemia, EPSEs at higher doses
QuetiapineAtypicalSedation, postural hypotension, weight gain
AripiprazoleD₂ partial agonistLess prolactin and weight gain; akathisia
ClozapineTreatment-resistant schizophrenia (after 2 antipsychotics, including 1 atypical)Agranulocytosis (mandatory FBC monitoring), myocarditis, severe constipation (ileus), hypersalivation, seizures, weight gain; levels rise when stopping smoking
  • Other risks: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion, very high CK: stop drug, cool, supportive, dantrolene)
    • QT prolongation
    • metabolic syndrome (monitor weight, BP, glucose/HbA1c, lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, yearly)
    • sedation
    • anticholinergic effects.
    • Long-acting injections (depots) help adherence.

los.text: Select psychological interventions in the management of various types of neurotic disorders.
sessions: Psychological therapies for mental health problems
los.html:
• NICE stepped care:
StepIntervention
1Recognition, assessment, psychoeducation, active monitoring
2Low-intensity: guided self-help (CBT-based), computerised CBT, psychoeducational groups (mild–moderate GAD, panic, mild OCD)
3High-intensity: individual CBT or applied relaxation; or medication (see LO 14)
4Specialist, complex care (combined treatment, crisis or inpatient)
DisorderPsychological treatment of choice
GADCBT or applied relaxation
Panic disorderCBT (including interoceptive exposure, challenging catastrophic thoughts)
Social anxietyIndividual CBT (Clark and Wells model)
Specific phobiaGraded exposure (systematic desensitisation using a fear hierarchy)
OCDCBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
PTSDTrauma-focused CBT or EMDR
DepressionCBT, behavioural activation, IPT; MBCT for relapse prevention
  • Access: primary care mental health services (in Wales, Local Primary Mental Health Support Services under the Mental Health (Wales) Measure 2010), online CBT (e.g. SilverCloud in Wales), NHS Talking Therapies in England.

los.text: Evaluate processes of assessing risk for patients and the public and concepts of 'patient compliance'.
sessions: The Mental Health Act and Mental Capacity Act
los.html:
• Risk assessment is a structured clinical judgement combining:
FactorExamples
Static (fixed)Previous attempts or violence, male sex, age, family history of suicide, childhood abuse
Dynamic (changeable)Current symptoms (hopelessness, command hallucinations), substance use, social crisis, non-adherence, access to means
ProtectiveSupport, children, faith, engagement with services, future plans
DomainsRisk to self (suicide, self-harm, neglect), to others (violence, children: safeguarding), from others (exploitation, abuse).
NICE (self-harm, 2022)
  • Don't use risk scales to predict suicide or decide who gets treatment
  • Do a psychosocial assessment focused on needs, with a safety plan.
Public protectionConfidentiality can be breached to prevent serious harm to others (GMC; W v Egdell); DVLA duties; MAPPA for offenders.
"Compliance" vs adherence vs concordanceCompliance implies obedience; adherence is how far behaviour matches agreed recommendations; concordance is a partnership with shared decisions.
Reasons for non-adherenceStrategies
  • Side effects, lack of insight, stigma, complex regimens, cognitive problems, substance misuse, beliefs about medicines, poor relationship with clinicians
  • Intentional or unintentional
Shared decision-making, psychoeducation, simplify regimens, manage side effects, depot antipsychotics, motivational interviewing, family involvement, reminders, Community Treatment Orders (MHA s17A) when necessary

los.text: Link factors in a history and mental state exam to abnormal moods and characteristic behaviours associated with psychotic depression and mania.
sessions: Classification and diagnosis of bipolar affective disorders
los.html:
Psychotic depressionMania
MoodSevere low mood, anhedonia, hopelessnessElevated or irritable mood, labile
ActivityPsychomotor retardation or agitation, stupor, food and fluid refusalIncreased energy and activity, reduced need for sleep, disinhibition (spending, sexual), risk-taking
Speech and thoughtSlow, sparse speechPressured speech, flight of ideas (rhyming, punning: clang associations), distractibility
Psychotic features (mood-congruent)Delusions of guilt, worthlessness, poverty, illness, nihilism (Cotard's: believing they're dead or rotting); derogatory voicesGrandiose delusions (special powers, identity, wealth), religious themes
AppearanceSelf-neglect, poor eye contactFlamboyant or inappropriate dress, overfamiliar
InsightOften poorPoor
RisksSuicide, dehydration and starvationFinancial ruin, sexual risk, exhaustion, accidents, aggression, exploitation
HypomaniaMilder (≥4 days), no psychosis, no marked impairment.
HistoryDuration, previous depressive and manic episodes, family history, triggers (sleep loss, antidepressants, steroids, substances, postpartum), collateral history.
Treatment
  • Psychotic depression → antidepressant + antipsychotic, or ECT if life-threatening
  • Mania → antipsychotic (haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone), stop antidepressants, then lithium or other mood stabiliser.

los.text: Link pathology to signs and symptoms of bipolar disorder.
sessions: Case presentation and mental state examination - mania
los.html:
• Bipolar disorder: bipolar I (≥1 manic episode), bipolar II (hypomania + major depression), cyclothymia (≥2 years of milder mood swings)
    • rapid cycling = ≥4 episodes a year
    • mixed features possible.
PathologyLink to symptoms
Genetics: very heritable (~70–85%), polygenicFamily history is a strong risk factor
Dopamine excess in mania (serotonin and noradrenaline changes in depression)Elation, energy, psychosis; antipsychotics treat mania
Circadian rhythm disruptionSleep loss triggers mania; reduced need for sleep
Intracellular signalling (inositol, GSK-3: inhibited by lithium)Mood stabilisation
HPA axis, inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunctionStress-related relapse
Brain changes: prefrontal grey matter loss, limbic (amygdala) dysregulationImpaired emotional regulation, impulsivity
Kindling: episodes become more frequent and less trigger-dependent over timeEarly, sustained treatment matters
  • Course: onset usually late teens to 20s
    • depression takes up most of the ill time
    • suicide risk is many times that of the general population.

los.text: Identify the indications, effects, side effects, interactions and contra-indications of medications (Lithium, anticonvulsants, benzodiazepines and antipsychotics,) ECT and psychosurgery.
los.html:
TreatmentKey points
Lithium
  • First-line long-term mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder (also acute mania, augmentation in resistant depression; reduces suicide).
  • Narrow therapeutic index: target 0.6–0.8 mmol/L (0.8–1.0 if relapsing), sampled 12 h after the dose
  • Weekly after starting or changing dose, then every 3 months (first year), then 6-monthly.
  • Baseline and 6-monthly U&E/eGFR, TFTs, calcium, weight
  • Prescribe by brand.
  • Side effects: fine tremor, polyuria/polydipsia (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, weight gain, long-term CKD, teratogenic (small Ebstein's risk).
  • Toxicity (>1.5): coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures, renal failure
  • Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, thiazides
  • Stop, IV fluids, haemodialysis if severe
AnticonvulsantsValproate (mania and prophylaxis; avoid in women who could become pregnant), lamotrigine (prevents bipolar depression; rash), carbamazepine (enzyme inducer)
AntipsychoticsAcute mania and prophylaxis (haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, aripiprazole); see LO 6 for side effects
Benzodiazepines
  • Positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A (↑ Cl⁻ channel opening frequency).
  • Uses: short-term anxiety or insomnia (2–4 weeks), alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, acute agitation, catatonia (lorazepam).
  • Risks: sedation, falls, cognitive impairment, respiratory depression with opioids or alcohol, paradoxical disinhibition, tolerance and dependence (withdrawal seizures: taper slowly), driving
  • Overdose → flumazenil (rarely, seizure risk)
Antidepressants in bipolar disorderOnly with an antimanic drug (risk of switching into mania); quetiapine, lamotrigine for bipolar depression
ECT
  • General anaesthetic + muscle relaxant, then an electrical stimulus to induce a brief seizure, usually twice weekly for 6–12 sessions.
  • Indications: severe life-threatening depression (stupor, food/fluid refusal, high suicide risk), psychotic depression, treatment resistance, catatonia, severe prolonged mania.
  • Side effects: anaesthetic risks, headache, myalgia, confusion, memory impairment (usually short-term; some autobiographical gaps persist).
  • Consent needed if capacity
  • If lacking capacity under the MHA, a SOAD must certify (s58A) and a valid advance refusal is binding except in an emergency
Psychosurgery
  • Neurosurgery for mental disorder (e.g. anterior capsulotomy, cingulotomy) for very refractory OCD or depression: extremely rare
  • MHA s57 requires consent and an independent second opinion
  • Deep brain stimulation experimental

los.text: Consolidate the learning objectives of the week and answer any residual questions. Neurotic Disorders- Case, Classification, Psychopathology, Aetiology, Pharmacological Treatment
los.html:
Casea 30-year-old with months of worry, tension and poor sleep, plus panic attacks on the bus.
Classification (ICD-11)
  • Anxiety or fear-related disorders (GAD, panic, agoraphobia, social anxiety, specific phobia, separation anxiety)
  • Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders (OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding)
  • Disorders specifically associated with stress (PTSD, complex PTSD, adjustment disorder)
  • Dissociative disorders
  • Bodily distress disorder.
PsychopathologyAnxiety has physical (autonomic: palpitations, sweating, tremor, breathlessness, GI upset), cognitive (worry, catastrophising, threat focus) and behavioural (avoidance, safety behaviours, reassurance seeking) components.
Aetiology(biopsychosocial)Genes, anxious temperament, early adversity, life stress, cognitive biases; maintaining factors (avoidance, safety behaviours, reassurance) are the targets of therapy.
  • Pharmacological treatment overview: SSRIs first line for most (sertraline for GAD)
  • SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine)
  • Pregabalin (GAD)
  • Clomipramine (OCD)
  • Propranolol (performance anxiety)
  • Benzodiazepines only short-term in crisis (see LO 14).
Prescribing points
  • Start low
  • Warn about initial jitteriness/anxiety
  • Effects after 2–4 weeks
  • Continue 6–12 months after remission (OCD longer)
  • Taper to stop (discontinuation symptoms, especially paroxetine and venlafaxine)
  • Watch for suicidal thoughts in under-25s
  • GI bleeding with NSAIDs (add a PPI)
  • Hyponatraemia in older people
  • Serotonin syndrome
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • QT (citalopram, escitalopram).

los.html:

FocusMany everyday worriesFear of the next attack, bodily sensationsNegative evaluation by othersOne object or situationIntrusive thoughts + ritualsA past trauma

AvoidanceLess prominent; reassurance seekingAgoraphobic placesSocial situationsThe triggerTriggers of obsessionsTrauma reminders

InsightPreservedPreservedPreservedPreservedUsually preservedPreserved

los.text: Select the pharmacological and other physical treatments in the management of neurotic disorders.
sessions: Aetiology and pharmacological treatment neurotic disorders
los.html:
DisorderFirst-line drug (NICE)Alternatives / other physical treatments
GADSertralineAnother SSRI or SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine), pregabalin; avoid long-term benzodiazepines
Panic disorderSSRIClomipramine or imipramine; no benzodiazepines (worse long-term outcomes)
Social anxietySSRI (escitalopram or sertraline)Venlafaxine; propranolol for performance-related physical symptoms
OCDSSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline, etc.) at higher doses for longerClomipramine; low-dose antipsychotic augmentation (aripiprazole, risperidone); deep brain stimulation or neurosurgery very rarely
PTSDPsychological therapy first; venlafaxine or an SSRI (sertraline) if preferredAntipsychotic (risperidone) adjunct for disabling symptoms; avoid benzodiazepines
  • Other physical approaches: regular exercise, sleep hygiene, cutting caffeine and alcohol, treating physical comorbidities
    • rTMS for depression (and OCD in some centres)
    • ECT is not used for anxiety disorders.

los.text: Explain Medical Law and Mental Health.
los.html:
LawKey provisions
Mental Health Act 1983 (amended 2007) (England and Wales)Detention for mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting hospital, for the person's health or safety or the protection of others
s2Assessment (± treatment) up to 28 days; 2 doctors (one s12-approved) + AMHP; not renewable
s3Treatment up to 6 months, renewable; 2 doctors + AMHP; appropriate treatment must be available
s4Emergency assessment, 72 h, 1 doctor + AMHP
s5(2)Doctor's holding power for an informal inpatient: 72 h
s5(4)Nurse's holding power: 6 h
s135 / s136Police powers: warrant to enter premises / remove a person from a public place to a place of safety (up to 24 h)
s17, s17ALeave; Community Treatment Order
s58, s58A, s57, s62Consent rules for medication after 3 months (consent or SOAD), ECT, psychosurgery, urgent treatment
s63Treatment of mental disorder without consent (not unrelated physical illness)
s117Free aftercare after s3
SafeguardsTribunal appeals (Mental Health Review Tribunal for Wales), IMHA advocacy, nearest relative rights
Mental Capacity Act 2005Decisions for people lacking capacity (including physical treatment of detained patients); DoLS for deprivation of liberty in care settings
Mental Health (Wales) Measure 2010Primary care mental health services, care and treatment plans, right to reassessment after discharge, advocacy for informal patients
Human Rights ActArticle 5 (liberty), Article 8 (private life)
  • Reform: a Mental Health Bill to update the 1983 Act (e.g. limiting detention of people with autism or learning disability, more patient choice) has been going through Parliament: check what's in force.

los.text: Discuss the variety of dilemmas that doctors have to deal with and strategies for decision making and procedure.
los.html:
DilemmaExample
Autonomy vs beneficenceA patient refuses treatment; capacity may fluctuate; mental illness doesn't automatically mean incapacity
Confidentiality vs protecting othersThreats to a named person; fitness to drive
CoercionDetention, restraint, rapid tranquillisation, covert medication
Physical illness in a detained patientMHA doesn't authorise unrelated physical treatment → MCA
Advance decisionsA bipolar patient's advance refusal ("Ulysses" wishes) can't override MHA treatment of mental disorder (except ECT refusals)
Pregnancy and medication, end-of-life decisions in severe anorexia, boundaries, stigma, resource allocation
  • Strategies:
    • Clarify the facts and the patient's views; assess capacity for the specific decision.
    • Apply ethical principles (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice) and frameworks.
    • Know the law (MHA, MCA, common law) and GMC guidance.
    • Choose the least restrictive option.
    • Consult: seniors, MDT, ethics committee, legal advisers, defence union; involve family and advocates.
    • Document reasoning; review; reflect and use supervision.

los.text: Identify current health innovations and their impact for clinical practice
los.html:
InnovationImpact
Digital therapies (online CBT such as SilverCloud in Wales, apps)Faster, scalable access; self-referral
Video consultations / telepsychiatryAccess for rural and housebound patients
Crisis lines (NHS 111 option 2 for mental health in Wales)24/7 urgent support
AI and digital phenotyping (wearables, sleep and activity data)Earlier relapse detection; ethical and privacy concerns
Novel treatments: rTMS, esketamine, psilocybin research, new antipsychotic mechanisms (muscarinic agonists), long-acting injectablesMore options for treatment resistance and adherence
Shared electronic recordsSafer, coordinated care
Peer support workers, social prescribingRecovery-focused, community care
  • Concerns: digital exclusion, data security, variable evidence quality and regulation, safety of unsupervised tools, loss of the therapeutic relationship, inequity.

los.text: Recognise and explain factors that contribute to a challenging consultation, including patient, clinician, and situational influences
los.html:
SourceFactors
Patient
  • Strong emotions (anger, distress, fear)
  • Mental illness
  • Intoxication or withdrawal
  • Cognitive impairment or delirium
  • Pain
  • Unmet or unrealistic expectations
  • Previous bad experiences
  • Language barriers
ClinicianFatigue, stress, time pressure, limited knowledge or confidence, own emotions and biases, burnout, poor communication
Situation / systemLong waits, delays, bad news, cancellations, complaints, noisy or unsafe rooms, lack of privacy, interruptions, third parties, organisational pressures, cultural differences

los.text: Evaluate the potential risks during a consultation, including emotional, clinical, or safety-related concerns
los.html:
RiskExamples / warning signs
EmotionalEscalating distress, re-traumatisation, clinician distress
ClinicalDiagnostic overshadowing: missing physical causes of agitation (hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, delirium, intoxication/withdrawal, head injury, sepsis, pain)
Safety (violence)Raised voice, swearing, pacing, clenched fists, staring, invading personal space, threats, previous violence, intoxication, weapons
EnvironmentExits, alarms, objects usable as weapons, lone working
  • Dynamic risk assessment throughout: sit where both you and the patient can reach an exit
    • know the alarm
    • tell colleagues
    • use a chaperone
    • leave if unsafe and call security or police.

los.text: Apply de-escalation techniques to help diffuse emotionally charged or confrontational consultations while maintaining professionalism
los.html:
De-escalation technique
Stay calm; slow, low, steady voice
Non-threatening body language: open posture, hands visible, side-on, keep more than an arm's length away, don't stare or touch
Introduce yourself, use their name, listen actively
Acknowledge and validate feelings ("I can see you're really frustrated about the wait")
Apologise for their experience where appropriate; don't argue, defend or blame
Offer choices rather than flat refusals; explain what you can do
Set boundaries calmly ("I want to help, but I can't while you're shouting")
Give time and space; find a shared goal; involve a senior
  • If it fails: prioritise safety, leave, call for help.
    • NICE NG10: de-escalation first
    • then oral PRN medication
    • then rapid tranquillisation (e.g. IM lorazepam, or haloperidol with promethazine)
    • restrictive interventions only as a last resort
    • debrief afterwards.

los.text: Reflect on and implement strategies to maintain personal wellbeing and support colleagues during and after challenging consultations
los.html:
• After a challenging consultation:
SelfColleagues
Debrief (hot debrief at the time; later reflective sessions, Schwartz rounds, Balint groups)Notice changes; ask "Are you OK?" and listen
Talk to a supervisor or trusted colleague; reflective writing (anonymised)Offer practical help (cover, breaks)
Basic self-care: sleep, food, breaks, exerciseInclude everyone in debriefs, including students
Recognise burnout (exhaustion, cynicism, reduced sense of achievement)Compassionate leadership, psychological safety
Seek help: occupational health, GP, Health for Health Professionals Wales, BMA support, counsellingSignpost support services
Report incidents of violence (Datix)Support reporting

los.text: Elicit a focused psychiatric history from a patient with symptoms suggestive of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
los.html:
AreaQuestions
TraumaWhat happened and when (only as much detail as they're comfortable sharing), single or repeated (complex PTSD)
Re-experiencingFlashbacks, intrusive memories, nightmares, distress and physical reactions to reminders
AvoidanceOf thoughts, conversations, places, people, activities
Sense of current threatHypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, poor concentration, sleep problems
Mood and beliefsGuilt, shame, self-blame, numbness, detachment, memory gaps
Duration and impactMore than a month; work, relationships, daily life
Complex PTSD featuresEmotional dysregulation, negative self-image, relationship difficulties (after prolonged trauma such as childhood or domestic abuse)
ComorbidityDepression, substance misuse (self-medication), anxiety, dissociation
RiskSuicide and self-harm, harm to others, ongoing danger (domestic abuse, safeguarding)
Support and treatmentPrevious therapy, support network
  • Trauma-informed approach: safety, choice, collaboration, trust, empowerment
    • let the patient control pace and detail
    • use grounding if they become distressed.
    • Screening: Trauma Screening Questionnaire, PCL-5.

los.text: Describe the core diagnostic features of PTSD, including re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal, and functional impact
los.html:
• ICD-11 PTSD: after exposure to an extremely threatening or horrific event:
Core clusterFeatures
Re-experiencing in the presentVivid intrusive memories, flashbacks, nightmares, with strong emotion and physical sensations
AvoidanceOf thoughts and memories, or activities, situations and people that are reminders
Persistent sense of current threatHypervigilance, enhanced startle
Functional impactLasts at least several weeks, causing significant impairment
DSM-5 adds negative changes in cognition and mood and requires >1 month.
Complex PTSDPTSD plus affect dysregulation, negative self-concept and relationship difficulties.
Acute stress reactionNormal distress lasting hours to days.
Risk factors
  • Severity and type (interpersonal violence, sexual assault), previous trauma, lack of support, pre-existing mental illness
  • Many exposed people recover without treatment.

los.text: Identify and explain evidence-based treatment options for PTSD, including psychological therapies and pharmacological management
los.html:
Option (NICE NG116)Use
Active monitoringMild symptoms in the first month
Trauma-focused CBT (individual, ~8–12 sessions; e.g. cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy for PTSD, prolonged exposure, narrative exposure)First line for adults (including within the first month if symptoms are significant) and children
EMDRAdults with non-combat trauma more than 3 months after the event
Supported computerised trauma-focused CBTAlternative for some
Complex PTSDLonger, phased therapy (stabilisation first)
Venlafaxine or an SSRI (e.g. sertraline)If the person prefers drug treatment or can't engage with therapy
Antipsychotic (risperidone)Adjunct for disabling symptoms (e.g. severe hyperarousal, psychotic symptoms)
AvoidBenzodiazepines; single-session psychological debriefing (may cause harm)
  • Also: practical and social support, treat comorbid depression and substance misuse (not a barrier to trauma therapy), specialist veterans' services (Veterans' NHS Wales).

los.text: Perform a structured and competent mental state examination (MSE), assessing cognitive, emotional, and behavioural aspects of the patient's presentation
los.html:
DomainDescribe objectively, with examples
Appearance and behaviourDress, hygiene, eye contact, rapport, psychomotor activity (agitation, retardation), abnormal movements, responding to unseen stimuli
SpeechRate, rhythm, volume, quantity, tone (pressured, slowed, monotonous, poverty)
MoodSubjective, in the patient's words ("I feel empty")
AffectObjective: range, reactivity, congruence (flat, blunted, labile, incongruent)
Thought formFlight of ideas, loosening of associations, tangentiality, thought block
Thought contentPreoccupations, delusions, obsessions, overvalued ideas, suicidal or homicidal ideation
PerceptionHallucinations (modality, person), illusions, depersonalisation
CognitionOrientation, attention, memory (formal tests if needed)
InsightAwareness of illness and need for treatment
RiskTo self, others, from others
  • Example: "Mr Z is a 45-year-old man, unkempt, with poor eye contact and psychomotor retardation.
    • His speech is slow and quiet with long pauses.
    • He describes his mood as 'hopeless'; his affect is flat and congruent.
    • Thought form is normal.
    • He expresses nihilistic beliefs that his insides are rotting and has passive suicidal thoughts without a plan.
    • He denies hallucinations.
    • He's orientated with impaired concentration.
    • Insight is partial."

los.text: Predict the effects of pathology on the anatomy of the renal system.
los.html:
PathologyAnatomical basisEffects you can predict
Kidney stonesThree narrowings: PUJ, pelvic brim, VUJColicky loin-to-groin pain (T11–L2, genitofemoral nerve to scrotum or labia); upstream hydronephrosis; infection above a block = emergency
PyelonephritisKidney under the 12th ribRenal angle tenderness, fever, rigors
Renal cell carcinomaLeft renal vein receives the left gonadal vein; tumour grows into renal vein and IVCHaematuria, loin pain, mass; left varicocele; IVC tumour thrombus; cannonball lung metastases
Polycystic kidneysLarge kidneys in the flanksBilateral ballotable masses, hypertension, CKD; berry aneurysms
AAA / retroperitoneal massUreters run on psoasUreteric obstruction; leaking AAA mimics renal colic
BPHTransition zone around the urethraVoiding symptoms, retention, back pressure → bilateral hydronephrosis and AKI
Bladder cancerUrothelium (shared with ureters and pelvis)Painless visible haematuria; may block a ureteric orifice
Bladder ruptureDome covered by peritoneum; base extraperitonealIntraperitoneal (blow to a full bladder) vs extraperitoneal (pelvic fracture)
Urethral injuryMembranous urethra fixed in the deep pouch; spongy urethra in the bulb
  • Pelvic fracture → blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate
  • Straddle injury → urine in the scrotum and abdominal wall, not thighs
Horseshoe kidneyFused lower poles trapped under the IMAStones, infection, obstruction
Neurogenic bladderS2–4, pontine centreCauda equina: painless retention with overflow; cord lesion: reflex bladder
  • Approach: follow the urine from the kidney to the meatus and ask where it can be blocked, what lies next to it, and which nerves carry its pain.

los.text: Predict the effects of pathology on the anatomy of the reproductive system
los.html:
PathologyAnatomical basisEffects you can predict
Testicular torsionBell-clapper testis; single testicular arterySudden pain (periumbilical referral, T10), high horizontal testis, lost cremasteric reflex; infarction within ~6 h
Testicular cancerLymph to para-aortic nodes (L1–2)Painless lump; nodes in the abdomen, not the groin; orchidectomy through an inguinal incision
VaricoceleLeft testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angleLeft-sided "bag of worms"; new one in an older man → check for a renal tumour
Hydrocele / indirect herniaProcessus vaginalisTransilluminates (hydrocele) vs can't get above it (hernia)
Prostate cancerPeripheral zone (felt on DRE); Batson's vertebral venous plexusHard craggy gland; bone metastases in the spine
Ectopic pregnancyAmpulla of the uterine tubePain, bleeding; rupture → haemoperitoneum in the pouch of Douglas, shoulder-tip pain
Ovarian torsion / cystOvary on the pelvic side wall beside the obturator nervePain referred to the medial thigh; torsion compromises the ovarian vessels in the suspensory ligament
Ovarian cancerLymph to para-aortic nodes; transcoelomic spreadAscites, omental cake, late presentation
Cervical cancerUreters ~2 cm lateral to the cervixSpread to the parametrium blocks the ureters → hydronephrosis, renal failure
Hysterectomy injuryUreter under the uterine arteryUreteric ligation or fistula
Uterovaginal prolapseLevator ani and endopelvic fascia (cardinal, uterosacral) weakened by childbirthCystocele, rectocele, uterine descent, stress incontinence
EndometriosisPouch of Douglas, uterosacral ligaments, ovariesDeep dyspareunia, dysmenorrhoea, fixed retroverted uterus
Breast cancerUpper outer quadrant, axillary nodes, Cooper's ligamentsLump, skin dimpling, peau d'orange, nipple retraction, axillary nodes
Pelvic inflammatory diseaseOpen path vagina → uterus → tubes → peritoneumTubal scarring (infertility, ectopic), Fitz-Hugh–Curtis (liver capsule)
